  • Do babies sleep in the womb? What movements and research tell us
Pregnancy

Do babies sleep in the womb? What movements and research tell us

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Babies develop sleep-like patterns before birth, but a kick does not always mean waking and a quiet spell cannot confirm safe sleep. Research offers clues about development while your baby’s usual movement pattern remains the practical focus.

Sleep-like states develop before birth

Yes, developing babies spend much of late pregnancy in states described as sleep. These states are part of a nervous system that is still maturing, so they are not simply a smaller version of an adult’s sleep schedule. Researchers infer them from patterns of movement, heart activity and other measurements.

You may notice that your baby often becomes active while you are resting in the evening or at another familiar time. Getting to know that pattern can be a meaningful part of pregnancy. It does not allow you to label every quiet moment as sleep or every kick as waking.

A statement that every baby sleeps exactly ninety-five percent of the time at thirty-eight to forty weeks is too precise for an individual pregnancy. Estimates depend on what was measured, for how long and how the state was classified. The practical priority is your baby’s usual movement pattern, not calculating a daily sleep percentage.

Fetal states are not the adult sleep-stage timetable

Researchers commonly describe quiet and active fetal sleep, alongside periods classified as quiet or active waking and transitional or indeterminate states. Eye movements, body movements and heart-rate patterns help distinguish them. Classification becomes clearer as pregnancy progresses; early development is harder to study.

Active sleep is associated with features such as rapid eye movements and spontaneous movements. Quiet sleep is generally less active. These observations do not justify applying an adult description of four non-REM stages followed by REM after exactly ninety minutes to a fetus.

Even the meaning of fetal wakefulness requires care: a measured behavioural state is not a direct report of conscious experience. The labels are useful for research and clinical interpretation, but parents cannot identify them reliably from a single movement or quiet spell.

Movement is not a simple sleep detector

A baby can move during active sleep. Small twitches, stretches and other movements are part of developing motor activity, so feeling a kick does not prove that your baby has just woken. Equally, feeling no movement for a while cannot establish that the baby is safely asleep.

Movement begins before it is strong enough for you to feel. First perceived movements commonly occur between sixteen and twenty-four weeks, sometimes later within that range in a first pregnancy. What you feel is only part of the activity taking place inside the uterus.

There is no expectation that every parent should feel fifty movements an hour. Activity varies, and being busy can make you less aware of it. Learn the pattern that is usual for your baby and follow your maternity team’s advice, rather than comparing with someone else’s counts.

What the human studies measured

A study published in 2010 examined 600 one-hour fetal heart-rate recordings from uncomplicated pregnancies between thirty and forty weeks. It found substantial variation in the time classified into different states. A recording can reveal physiological patterns, but a single hour is not a complete twenty-four-hour sleep diary.

A much smaller paper in a 2008 journal issue followed ten low-risk pregnancies and the same babies after birth. It compared fetal electrocardiographic recordings, which measure electrical heart activity, with newborn polysomnography, a broader sleep recording. The investigators reported partial continuity between fetal and newborn sleep measures.

The newborns spent less time in the measured sleep states than before birth, and some state proportions had negative correlations. This is more complicated than saying “more fetal sleep means a better sleeper”. A study of ten babies with different prenatal and postnatal measurements cannot forecast how long your newborn will sleep at home.

Why researchers also study fetal sheep

Measuring the developing human brain continuously inside the uterus has practical and ethical limits. Animal studies allow some measurements that would not be appropriate in a human pregnancy. They can help investigate how immature brain activity becomes organised, while still leaving questions about how closely the findings apply to people.

A 2009 study used recordings from the surface of the brain, called electrocorticography, to examine activity in fetal sheep at about seventy percent of gestation, before mature organised sleep states had developed. The analysis compared these early patterns with findings from later gestation.

This work concerns the emergence of brain-activity organisation. It does not establish the exact week that a human fetus first sleeps, and it cannot show that a fetus is dreaming about a particular experience. Sheep research should be described as an animal model rather than presented as direct observation of a human baby.

What newborn movements may reveal about brain development

A 2018 study examined nineteen newborns, including preterm and term babies, at thirty-one to forty-two corrected gestational weeks. Researchers recorded isolated hand movements during active sleep and the associated patterns of brain activity. The movement-related signals changed as the babies matured.

These observations support the idea that spontaneous movement provides useful sensory input to the developing brain. However, the recordings were made after birth, even when a premature baby’s developmental age corresponded to a stage normally spent in the womb.

The findings do not mean that stronger kicks prove better brain development or that parents should stimulate extra movements. They help scientists explore how sensory and motor systems develop together. A parent’s job is not to produce a certain quantity of fetal exercise or sleep.

The brain and senses continue developing during quiet periods

The foundations of the nervous system form early in pregnancy. Around gestational week five, the neural tube is developing into the structures that will become the brain and spinal cord. Pregnancy weeks are usually counted from the last menstrual period, so they are not the same as weeks since conception.

Brain growth and increasing complexity continue throughout pregnancy. Taste-related structures and hearing also develop gradually, and the amniotic environment provides sensory exposures. Substances related to the pregnant person’s diet can influence the flavour environment, while sounds such as the maternal voice become part of later prenatal experience.

A response to sound or another stimulus does not tell us exactly what the fetus understands or consciously recognises. You can talk or sing naturally if you enjoy it, without testing for a response on demand. Quietness does not mean that development has paused, and sensory development does not require a home stimulation programme.

Do babies dream in the womb?

We do not know whether fetal sleep includes dreams like those described by older children and adults. Rapid eye movements and an active-sleep pattern cannot reveal the contents of an experience, and a fetus cannot report what it is feeling.

It can be enjoyable to imagine what your baby might be experiencing, but those images are speculation rather than a scientific finding. Pregnancy cravings do not show that the baby is dreaming about food. The evidence is stronger for developing sleep and sensory functions than for claims about dream content.

Keeping that distinction does not make the pregnancy less personal. You can feel connected to a baby whose inner experience is still largely unknown, while using observable movement changes and professional care to monitor wellbeing.

Fetal sleep does not promise long nights after birth

A baby’s environment changes greatly at birth, including feeding, temperature, light and contact with caregivers. Newborns spend much of the day and night asleep, but their sleep is broken into shorter periods. They need frequent feeding and do not begin life with an adult day-and-night routine.

An active fetus is not necessarily going to be a restless newborn, and a quiet-looking fetal pattern does not guarantee long stretches of sleep. Studies of developmental continuity describe groups and physiological measurements, not a prediction for an individual family’s nights.

After birth, follow the care team’s feeding and growth advice rather than stretching sleep because the baby seemed to sleep for long periods before delivery. Ask for help if a newborn is unusually hard to wake or not feeding well; that is a health concern, not simply a desirable sleep habit.

A change in movements should not be explained away as sleep

Babies have quieter periods, but a possible sleep cycle is not a reason to delay reporting reduced movement. Contact your midwife or maternity unit immediately if your baby is moving less than usual, stops moving or has a change in the usual pattern. Do not wait until the next day, even during the night.

If you have never felt movement by twenty-four weeks, tell your maternity team. As the due date approaches, the type of movement can change, but you should continue to feel your baby move up to and during labour. Do not assume there is too little room for movement to matter.

A home Doppler or heartbeat-listening app cannot establish that the baby is well. Nor should attempts to wake the baby with food, drinks or stimulation delay a call about a concerning change. The maternity team can assess the situation according to the stage of pregnancy and your baby’s history.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fetal states are developing patterns, not an adult sleep timetable.

Animal and newborn studies do not directly measure every aspect of human fetal experience.

Reduced or changed movements need immediate maternity advice.

How BeMama can help

Get to know the pattern that is usual for your baby and keep your maternity contact number available. Enjoy talking or singing without trying to test or control sleep.

When to seek help

Contact your maternity unit immediately for reduced, absent or changed movements. Do not wait for a presumed sleep cycle to end or rely on a home heartbeat device.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Movement can occur during active sleep.
  • There is no universal fifty-movements-per-hour target.
  • Sleep research does not reveal fetal dreams.
  • Small studies cannot predict newborn sleep for a family.
  • A movement change needs assessment, not a sleep explanation.

Frequently asked questions

Does a kick prove my baby is awake?

No. Movement can also occur during active sleep.

Does a quiet spell prove my baby is safely asleep?

No. A change from the usual movement pattern needs immediate maternity advice.

Do fetuses follow the adult ninety-minute sleep timetable?

No. Developing fetal states should not be mapped directly onto adult sleep stages or a fixed timetable.

Should I feel fifty movements every hour?

No. There is no universal movement count that every baby must meet.

Did the 2008 study predict how well each baby would sleep at home?

No. It involved ten babies and physiological measurements, not a reliable forecast of a family’s newborn sleep.

Was the 2009 brain-recording study done in human fetuses?

No. It studied fetal sheep, so it cannot be presented as direct evidence of human dreams or an exact human sleep milestone.

Were the nineteen babies in the 2018 movement study still in the womb?

No. The recordings were made after birth in preterm and term newborns.

Do pregnancy cravings reveal what my baby dreams about?

No. Dream content cannot be inferred from cravings or fetal movements.

Will lots of fetal sleep mean long uninterrupted newborn nights?

No. Newborn feeding and sleep needs differ from the prenatal environment.

Should I wait until morning if movements are reduced?

No. Contact your maternity unit immediately, even during the night.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
